name: iPhone & Mobile Browser Capability Checker
title: iPhone & Mobile Browser Capability Checker (ProMotion, DPR, Safe Areas) | Toolkit Gen
description: Benchmark mobile browser display capabilities: test physical pixels vs CSS points, Display P3 color gamut, ProMotion 120Hz refresh rates, notch/safe-area insets, and Safari Web API support.
author: ToolkitGen Engineering Team
quickAnswer: The iPhone & Mobile Browser Capability Checker audits mobile screen geometry, color accuracy, and browser rendering capabilities. It calculates true physical pixels versus CSS viewport points ($dpr = \text{window.devicePixelRatio}$), checks for Wide Color Display P3 and HDR dynamic range headroom, detects delivered animation refresh rates, explains why Safari for iOS caps animations at 60Hz on 120Hz ProMotion screens, renders interactive notch and Dynamic Island safe-area insets, and benchmarks support for modern Web APIs. All diagnostics execute locally in browser memory.

faq.q: Why does my 120Hz iPhone Pro display 60Hz in Safari?
faq.a: Apple WebKit intentionally throttles requestAnimationFrame to 60Hz in Safari on iOS to conserve battery life, even on devices equipped with 120Hz ProMotion displays (iPhone 13 Pro through 16 Pro). This limit is governed by the internal WebKit feature flag 'Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps'. You can unlock full 120Hz web rendering by opening iOS Settings > Apps > Safari > Advanced > Feature Flags, toggling 'Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps' to OFF, and restarting Safari [Confirmed: WebKit Bugzilla, Apple Developer].

faq.q: What is the difference between physical pixels and CSS points on iPhone?
faq.a: Physical pixels represent the microscopic organic light-emitting diode (OLED) sub-pixel clusters on the hardware glass. CSS points represent the logical coordinates used by web layouts. Modern iPhones utilize a 3x Device Pixel Ratio ($dpr = 3.0$), meaning each logical point comprises a 3-by-3 grid of 9 physical sub-pixel units. For example, the iPhone 15 Pro features 393 x 852 CSS points, mapping to 1179 x 2556 physical pixels.

faq.q: Why doesn't Safari support WebHID or Web Bluetooth?
faq.a: Apple's WebKit security and privacy team has consistently declined to implement the WebHID, WebUSB, and Web Bluetooth APIs in iOS Safari. Apple cites user fingerprinting risks, peripheral side-channel attacks, and potential security vulnerabilities in connected accessories as reasons for omitting these hardware connection APIs.

Safe-area insets are standardized CSS environment variables—env(safe-area-inset-top), env(safe-area-inset-bottom), env(safe-area-inset-left), and env(safe-area-inset-right)—that specify padding values needed to keep interactive buttons, text, and navigation bars from being obscured by hardware notches, the Dynamic Island pill, or the iOS home indicator bar.

How to Unlock 120Hz ProMotion in Safari on iOS:
  1. Open the Settings app on your iPhone or iPad.
  2. Scroll down and tap Apps > Safari (or Safari directly on iOS 17 and earlier).
  3. Scroll to the bottom and tap Advanced > Feature Flags (or Experimental Features).
  4. Locate the toggle named Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps.
  5. Turn this toggle OFF.
  6. Swipe up to close Safari from the app switcher, then reopen this page to enjoy fluid 120Hz ProMotion rendering.

articleHtml:
Mobile Display Architecture, ProMotion Refresh Timing, and WebKit API Boundaries

Modern smartphones feature custom silicon, variable refresh displays, and wide color gamuts that rival professional reference monitors. However, developers and users frequently encounter unexpected differences between native application performance and web browser execution, particularly on Apple iOS devices.

Device Pixel Ratios: Logical Points versus Physical OLED Sub-Pixels

When Steve Jobs introduced the Retina display in 2010, Apple decoupled physical screen hardware pixels from web layout dimensions. If web browsers rendered layouts strictly based on physical pixels on a modern 1179 x 2556 smartphone screen, website buttons and text would appear microscopic.

To preserve tactile ergonomics, mobile operating systems define logical CSS points. The translation between logical points and physical hardware pixels is governed by the Device Pixel Ratio ($dpr$):

$$\text{Physical Pixels} = \text{CSS Points} \times \text{window.devicePixelRatio}$$

Modern flagship iPhones (iPhone 13 Pro through iPhone 16 Pro) standardize on a $3.0\times$ multiplier. A 393-point wide viewport corresponds to exactly 1,179 physical horizontal pixel lines. When authoring images or canvas graphics for high-density mobile screens, providing $3\times$ asset resolutions (e.g. @3x) ensures razor-sharp rendering on Super Retina XDR OLED displays.

The ProMotion 120Hz Conundrum in Safari for iOS

Apple introduced 120Hz ProMotion displays to the iPhone line with the iPhone 13 Pro in 2021. In native iOS applications, UI scrolling and animations smoothly ramp up to 120 updates per second via the system CADisplayLink timer. However, users running web applications or high-framerate HTML5 animations in Safari frequently discover that animations remain locked at 60 frames per second.

This limitation is not a hardware defect; it is an intentional power-conservation policy enforced by Apple WebKit engineers [Confirmed: WebKit Bugzilla]. Inside WebKit, a feature flag named Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps is enabled by default. This flag throttles the browser's requestAnimationFrame loop to 60Hz to prevent web pages with poorly optimized JavaScript loops from rapidly draining the device battery.

Users who require true 120Hz web rendering (such as web game players, 3D modelers, and interactive telemetry users) can manually disable this throttle. In iOS Settings > Apps > Safari > Advanced > Feature Flags, turning off 'Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps' immediately releases the 60Hz ceiling, allowing Safari to deliver full 120Hz frame pacing.

Wide Color Gamut: Display P3 versus sRGB

Standard web content historically targeted the sRGB color space, established in 1996 for CRT monitors. Modern Apple displays, by contrast, are calibrated to the wider Display P3 color space, which encompasses approximately 25% more visible color volume than sRGB—particularly across saturated reds, vibrant greens, and deep oranges.

Modern CSS allows developers to deliver wide-gamut colors conditionally via media queries and the CSS Color Module Level 4:

@media (color-gamut: p3) {
  .brand-accent { color: color(display-p3 0.95 0.28 0.18); }
}

When viewed on an iPhone or MacBook with an OLED or Mini-LED panel, P3 colors appear noticeably more vivid without clipping shadow details.

The Web API Gap: WebKit Restrictions on Mobile Hardware

On Android devices, Google Chrome and other Chromium-based browsers grant web applications broad access to connected hardware through the Project Fugu initiative. On iOS, however, Apple requires all alternative browsers (including Chrome and Firefox) to utilize the WebKit rendering engine under App Store guideline 2.5.6.

As a result, several powerful modern Web APIs are completely unsupported on iOS devices:

  • WebHID (Human Interface Devices): Prohibits web applications from reading raw USB or Bluetooth gamepad reports directly, requiring developers to rely on the standard Gamepad API.
  • Web Bluetooth: Prohibits web apps from establishing wireless connections to BLE beacons, heart rate monitors, or Arduino microcontrollers.
  • File System Access API: Prevents websites from reading or writing directly to user-selected device folders. (WebKit does support the Origin Private File System (OPFS), which allows high-performance virtual storage isolated from user view).
  • WebUSB & Web Serial: Disallows direct serial baud communication with external diagnostic hardware or 3D printers.

Conversely, Apple has introduced native support for WebGPU in iOS 17 and macOS Sonoma, enabling compute shaders, local machine learning models, and complex 3D rasterization directly inside Safari.
